segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Miss Judith Vane came to Mrs Copp's on Friday morning with nothing in her hands and no errand from the shop, which was unlike her.

segments.speaker: Miss Judith Vane
segments.text: I heard six words in your passage a fortnight ago. Until she goes, and then let it lapse. I have told nobody, and I shall not.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Margaret folded her hands and said nothing at all.

segments.speaker: Miss Judith Vane
segments.text: I came because Mrs Pike has been telling the green all week that you and Mr Dene have quarrelled.

segments.speaker: Miss Margaret Selby
segments.text: He told the Bramdean master he would put an end to it the day my aunt takes the coach.

segments.speaker: Miss Judith Vane
segments.text: Yes. To the pretence.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Margaret looked up.

segments.speaker: Miss Judith Vane
segments.text: He said he had had the good of it and never earned a shilling of it. A man does not speak of a woman's regard as a debt unless he minds very much about the owing.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: There was a silence in which the kitchen clock was extremely audible.

segments.speaker: Miss Margaret Selby
segments.text: You might have left me in it.

segments.speaker: Miss Judith Vane
segments.text: I dislike a story that does not add up, and this one has not added up since Monday the ninth.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: She went down the green towards her brother's shop and told nobody there either.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Margaret reached the schoolroom before eleven, with her bonnet strings loose. Dene was alone at the long desk, ruling a line in the coal account.

segments.speaker: Miss Margaret Selby
segments.text: What did you mean to put an end to?

segments.speaker: Mr Robert Dene
segments.text: The lie. What else was there?

segments.speaker: Miss Margaret Selby
segments.text: I thought you meant me.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He put the pen down and came round the desk.

segments.speaker: Mr Robert Dene
segments.text: I meant to say it to you honestly, once, with nobody arranging us. I have been eleven days trying to find a quarter of an hour when Mrs Pike was not at the window.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He had her hand by then, and she had let him take it. Neither of them heard the latch.

segments.speaker: Mrs Honoria Pike
segments.text: There! And they said they had quarrelled.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Mrs Ferris came in past her and set her gloves down on the nearest desk.

segments.speaker: Mrs Augusta Ferris
segments.text: Mr Dene. My niece has eighteen pounds a year and a turned gown. If I settle not one shilling on her, would you marry her?

segments.speaker: Mr Robert Dene
segments.text: Yes.

segments.speaker: Mrs Augusta Ferris
segments.text: On forty pounds a year.

segments.speaker: Mr Robert Dene
segments.text: On forty pounds a year, in two rooms, with the coal account unpaid. I would rather have her penniless and honestly mine than take her with your money and spend my life knowing which of us had bought the marriage. I am poor. I am not for sale.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Mrs Ferris looked at him over the top of her spectacles. She had put that question once before, to a young man in Bath in the year nine, over eight hundred pounds, and he had taken until the morning to answer it.

segments.speaker: Mrs Augusta Ferris
segments.text: Well. Something has happened here after all.

segments.speaker: Mrs Honoria Pike
segments.text: Of course something has happened. I have been saying so since Easter.
